claim: Recent developments in neural interfaces enable the real-time and non-invasive tracking of motor neuron spiking activity.
source: Recent developments in neural interfaces enable the real-time and non-invasive tracking of motor neuron spiking activity.
evidence: This is a statement about technological capabilities in the field, presented as established fact in the abstract.

claim: Seven human subjects participated in the study (N = 7).
source: Here, we provided human subjects (N = 7) with real-time feedback on the discharge patterns of pairs of motor units (MUs) innervating a single muscle (tibialis anterior) and encouraged them to independently control the MUs by tracking targets in a 2D space.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of subjects in the study.

claim: Subjects were provided with real-time feedback on the discharge patterns of pairs of motor units innervating the tibialis anterior muscle.
source: Here, we provided human subjects (N = 7) with real-time feedback on the discharge patterns of pairs of motor units (MUs) innervating a single muscle (tibialis anterior) and encouraged them to independently control the MUs by tracking targets in a 2D space.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental method used.

claim: Subjects learned control strategies to achieve the target-tracking task for various combinations of motor units.
source: Subjects learned control strategies to achieve the target-tracking task for various combinations of MUs.
evidence: Statement of experimental outcome in the abstract.

claim: The control strategies rarely corresponded to volitional control of independent input signals to individual motor units during the onset of neural activity.
source: These strategies rarely corresponded to a volitional control of independent input signals to individual MUs during the onset of neural activity.
evidence: Key finding stated in the abstract regarding the nature of control strategies.

claim: Motor unit activation was consistent with a common input to the motor unit pair.
source: Conversely, MU activation was consistent with a common input to the MU pair, while individual activation of the MUs in the pair was predominantly achieved by alterations in de-recruitment order that could be explained by history-dependent changes in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Main finding stated in the abstract about the mechanism of motor unit activation.

claim: Individual activation of motor units in the pair was predominantly achieved by alterations in de-recruitment order.
source: Conversely, MU activation was consistent with a common input to the MU pair, while individual activation of the MUs in the pair was predominantly achieved by alterations in de-recruitment order that could be explained by history-dependent changes in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Main finding about how individual motor unit activation was achieved.

claim: Alterations in de-recruitment order could be explained by history-dependent changes in motor neuron excitability.
source: Conversely, MU activation was consistent with a common input to the MU pair, while individual activation of the MUs in the pair was predominantly achieved by alterations in de-recruitment order that could be explained by history-dependent changes in motor neuron excitability.
evidence: Interpretation of the mechanism underlying the observed de-recruitment patterns.

claim: Flexible motor unit recruitment based on independent synaptic inputs to single motor units is unlikely.
source: These results suggest that flexible MU recruitment based on independent synaptic inputs to single MUs is unlikely, although de-recruitment might reflect varying inputs or modulations in the neuron's intrinsic excitability.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results stated in the abstract.

claim: De-recruitment might reflect varying inputs or modulations in the neuron's intrinsic excitability.
source: These results suggest that flexible MU recruitment based on independent synaptic inputs to single MUs is unlikely, although de-recruitment might reflect varying inputs or modulations in the neuron's intrinsic excitability.
evidence: Alternative interpretation offered for de-recruitment patterns.

claim: Decoding single motor unit spiking activity non-invasively from surface EMG represents a viable alternative to invasive brain recordings for neural human-machine interfaces.
source: Decoding single motor unit (MU) spiking activity, that is, action potentials discharged by motor neurons and their innervated muscle fibres, non-invasively from the surface electromyogram (EMG), represents a viable alternative to invasive brain recordings for neural human–machine interfaces (Holobar and Farina, 2021; Formento et al., 2021; Farina and Holobar, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Hundreds to thousands of motor neurons innervate muscles.
source: One potential application for such non-invasive neural interfaces is to augment the number of degrees of freedom a person can control by exploiting the fact that hundreds to thousands of motor neurons innervate muscles (Heckman and Enoka, 2012).
evidence: Anatomical fact supported by citation.

claim: Single motor units tend to be activated in a stereotyped way determined by common input received by functional groups of motor units.
source: Indeed, most previous observations indicate that, contrary to independent control, single MUs tend to be activated in a very stereotyped way which is determined by the common input received by functional groups of MUs (Negro et al., 2016b; Tanzarella et al., 2021; Farina et al., 2014) and by their biophysical properties (i.e. Henneman's size principle stating a dependency between the exerted force at which an MU starts to contribute and the neuron's size; Henneman, 1957; Henneman et al., 1974).
evidence: Statement about motor unit activation patterns supported by multiple citations.

claim: Henneman's size principle states a dependency between the exerted force at which a motor unit starts to contribute and the neuron's size.
source: Indeed, most previous observations indicate that, contrary to independent control, single MUs tend to be activated in a very stereotyped way which is determined by the common input received by functional groups of MUs (Negro et al., 2016b; Tanzarella et al., 2021; Farina et al., 2014) and by their biophysical properties (i.e. Henneman's size principle stating a dependency between the exerted force at which an MU starts to contribute and the neuron's size; Henneman, 1957; Henneman et al., 1974).
evidence: Definition of Henneman's size principle with citations.

claim: The size of the soma is inversely related to the membrane resistance.
source: Since the size of the soma is inversely related to the membrane resistance, smaller motor neurons discharge action potentials earlier and at higher rates than larger neurons for the same net excitatory synaptic input (Stein et al., 2005).
evidence: Biophysical relationship stated with citation.

claim: Smaller motor neurons discharge action potentials earlier and at higher rates than larger neurons for the same net excitatory synaptic input.
source: Since the size of the soma is inversely related to the membrane resistance, smaller motor neurons discharge action potentials earlier and at higher rates than larger neurons for the same net excitatory synaptic input (Stein et al., 2005).
evidence: Physiological consequence of soma size with citation.

claim: The size principle has been observed in several muscles.
source: The size principle has been observed in several muscles (Desmedt and Godaux, 1977a; Oya et al., 2009; van Zuylen et al., 1988; Thomas et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1986; Monster and Chan, 1977) and appears to remain robust in various scenarios (Thomas et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1986; Adam and De Luca, 2003; Fling et al., 2009; Desmedt and Godaux, 1977b; Thomas et al., 1978; Jones et al., 1994).
evidence: Empirical observation supported by multiple citations.

claim: The size principle appears to remain robust in various scenarios.
source: The size principle has been observed in several muscles (Desmedt and Godaux, 1977a; Oya et al., 2009; van Zuylen et al., 1988; Thomas et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1986; Monster and Chan, 1977) and appears to remain robust in various scenarios (Thomas et al., 1987; Thomas et al., 1986; Adam and De Luca, 2003; Fling et al., 2009; Desmedt and Godaux, 1977b; Thomas et al., 1978; Jones et al., 1994).
evidence: Statement about the robustness of the size principle supported by citations.

claim: There is evidence for a neural substrate that would allow for selective cortical control of motor units via descending pathways.
source: A recent study even provided evidence that indeed there is, to some degree, a neural substrate that would allow for the selective cortical control of MUs via descending pathways (Marshall et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about neural substrate supported by citation.

claim: On average, 11.04 ± 3.34 motor units were reliably decomposed per subject.
source: During the main experimental sessions, on average, 11.04 ± 3.34 MUs were reliably decomposed (online surface EMG decomposition) per subject (N = 7).
evidence: Quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: The order in which motor units are de-recruited often differed from the recruitment order.
source: As indicated by the green and red marks, the order in which MUs are de-recruited often differed from the recruitment order.
evidence: Observation from experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Once recruited, a motor unit could keep discharging action potentials even when the exerted force level was below the initial recruitment threshold.
source: For example, once recruited, an MU could keep discharging action potentials even when the exerted force level was below the initial recruitment threshold.
evidence: Specific observation about motor unit behavior during the experiment.

claim: Recruitment and de-recruitment threshold of the selected motor units showed a strong relationship across days and subjects (Spearman's correlation coefficient, R = 0.53, p<0.001).
source: Recruitment and de-recruitment threshold of the selected MUs showed a strong relationship across days and subjects (Spearman's correlation coefficient, R = 0.53, p<0.001; see Figure 1C).
evidence: Statistical result from data analysis with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: On average, the de-recruitment threshold was –1.11 ± 2.44% maximum voluntary contraction smaller than the recruitment threshold.
source: On average, the de-recruitment threshold was –1.11 ± 2.44% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) smaller than the recruitment one, and in 66.7% a selected MU was de-recruited at a force level below its initial recruitment threshold.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental measurements.

claim: In 66.7% of cases, a selected motor unit was de-recruited at a force level below its initial recruitment threshold.
source: On average, the de-recruitment threshold was –1.11 ± 2.44% maximum voluntary contraction (MVC) smaller than the recruitment one, and in 66.7% a selected MU was de-recruited at a force level below its initial recruitment threshold.
evidence: Quantitative result from experimental data.

claim: The overall observed effect of de-recruitment threshold being lower than recruitment threshold was weak (p=0.111).
source: The overall observed effect, however, was weak (see Materials and methods, p=0.111).
evidence: Statistical result indicating the strength of the observed effect.

claim: The target hit rate improved from the first to the last day of training from 41.19 ± 17.76% to 67.04 ± 18.17% (p=0.028).
source: The target hit rate improved from the first to the last day of training from 41.19 ± 17.76% to 67.04 ± 18.17% (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.028).
evidence: Statistical result showing improvement in performance over training.

claim: The angle hit rate improved from 64.37 ± 13.15% to 81.11 ± 9.84% (p=0.016).
source: A similar trend was observed for the angle hits with an improvement from 64.37 ± 13.15% to 81.11 ± 9.84% (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical result showing improvement in angle hits over training.

claim: Performance per subject across targets and conditions improved from the first to the last day of training from 0.56 ± 0.09 to 0.69 ± 0.10 (p=0.016).
source: According to the distanced-based performance metric (defined in Materials and methods), the performance per subject across targets and conditions improved from the first to the last day of training from 0.56 ± 0.09 to 0.69 ± 0.10 (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical result showing overall performance improvement.

claim: The performance in hitting TI did not significantly improve from the first day of training to the last day (from 0.67 ± 0.18 to 0.68 ± 0.11; p=0.938).
source: The performance in hitting TI did not significantly improve from the first day of training to the last day (from 0.67 ± 0.18 to 0.68 ± 0.11; two-sided Wilcoxon singed-rank test, p=0.938).
evidence: Statistical result showing no significant improvement for target TI.

claim: No significant improvement was observed for TII (from 0.69 ± 0.11 to 0.80 ± 0.13; p=0.109).
source: Similarly, no significant improvement was observed for TII (from 0.69 ± 0.11 to 0.80 ± 0.13; two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.109).
evidence: Statistical result showing no significant improvement for target TII.

claim: A significant improvement in performance was detected when subjects were asked to move towards TIII (from 0.33 ± 0.12 to 0.59 ± 0.17; p=0.016).
source: However, a significant improvement in performance was detected when subjects were asked to move towards TIII (from 0.33 ± 0.12 to 0.59 ± 0.17; two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical result showing significant improvement for target TIII.

claim: Only minor within-session learning was found across conditions and days.
source: Furthermore, across conditions and days, we only found minor within-session learning (mean correlation between performance and consecutive trials across days and condition for TI: 0.037 ± 0.078, TII: 0.066 ± 0.094, TIII: 0.043 ± 0.074, see Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) with no significant difference across targets (Friedman, p=0.103).
evidence: Statistical result about within-session learning with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: Performance per subject in reaching TI significantly increased from selected motor unit pairs with a small difference in recruitment threshold (0–1% MVC) to those with a high difference (3–10% MVC) from 0.61 ± 0.16 to 0.90 ± 0.05 (p=0.016).
source: Performance per subject in reaching TI significantly increased from selected MU pairs with a small difference in recruitment threshold (0–1% MVC) to those with a high difference (3–10% MVC) from 0.61 ± 0.16 to 0.90 ± 0.05 (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical result showing relationship between performance and recruitment threshold difference.

claim: For TII, no dependency in performance and the within-pair difference in recruitment threshold was detected (from 0.79 ± 0.07 to 0.72 ± 0.08, p=0.578).
source: For TII, no dependency in performance and the within-pair difference in recruitment threshold was detected (from 0.79 ± 0.07 to 0.72 ± 0.08, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.578).
evidence: Statistical result showing no relationship for target TII.

claim: The performance in reaching TIII decreased significantly for larger differences in recruitment threshold within the selected motor unit pair from 0.66 ± 0.09 to 0.55 ± 0.04 (p=0.016).
source: On the contrary, the performance in reaching TIII decreased significantly for larger differences in recruitment threshold within the selected MU pair from 0.66 ± 0.09 to 0.55 ± 0.04 (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p=0.016).
evidence: Statistical result showing inverse relationship for target TIII.

claim: The difference in recruitment threshold between MU1 and MU2 correlated with the difference in de-recruitment threshold (Spearman's correlation coefficient, R=0.46, p=0.001).
source: The difference in recruitment threshold between MU1 and MU2 correlated with the difference in de-recruitment threshold (Spearman's correlation coefficient, R=0.46, p=0.001; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical result showing correlation between recruitment and de-recruitment thresholds.

claim: The majority of subjects reported that they felt having control over MU2 when reaching towards TIII (14% of cases subjects indicated having no control over MU2).
source: During the last 5 days of training, the majority subjects reported that they felt having control over MU2 when reaching towards TIII (14% of cases subjects indicated having no control over MU2; see Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Subjective report from questionnaire data.

claim: In 95% of all cases, subjects declared the usage of a clear strategy to establish control over MU2.
source: Moreover, they declared the usage of a clear strategy to establish such control, which varied in cognitive demand across subjects and days. In 95% of all cases, this control strategy was described as a rapid increase in force due to dorsiflexion of the ankle followed by a slow release until the cursor moves towards the vertical axis.
evidence: Subjective report from questionnaire data.

claim: The control strategy was described as a rapid increase in force due to dorsiflexion of the ankle followed by a slow release until the cursor moves towards the vertical axis.
source: In 95% of all cases, this control strategy was described as a rapid increase in force due to dorsiflexion of the ankle followed by a slow release until the cursor moves towards the vertical axis.
evidence: Description of control strategy from questionnaire responses.

claim: During the last 5 days of training, 76, 78, and 94% of all successful attempts of going towards TI were achieved without activating MU2 once during the trial in conditions I, II, and III, respectively.
source: In fact, during the last 5 days of training, 76, 78, and 94% of all successful attempts, that is, at least an angle hit, of going towards TI were achieved without activating MU2 once during the trial while it was only 7, 2, and 1% for TIII (MU2 only without MU1) in conditions I, II, and III, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative result showing frequency of direct movements to targets.

claim: Only 7, 2, and 1% of successful attempts towards TIII were achieved with MU2 only without MU1 in conditions I, II, and III, respectively.
source: In fact, during the last 5 days of training, 76, 78, and 94% of all successful attempts, that is, at least an angle hit, of going towards TI were achieved without activating MU2 once during the trial while it was only 7, 2, and 1% for TIII (MU2 only without MU1) in conditions I, II, and III, respectively.
evidence: Quantitative result showing rarity of direct movements to TIII.

claim: All subjects moved directly towards TI in more than 70% of all successful attempts.
source: Also, all subjects moved directly towards TI in more than 70% of all successful attempts.
evidence: Quantitative result about direct movement patterns across subjects, referenced with Figure 5C.

claim: Only three subjects navigated the cursor directly towards TIII in more than 5% of all successful attempts.
source: Although only three subjects navigated the cursor directly towards TIII in more than 5% of all successful attempts (see Figure 5C).
evidence: Quantitative result about direct movement patterns, referenced with Figure 5C.

claim: 8.33% of direct movements towards TIII occurred after TI-instructed trials.
source: Furthermore, 8.33% of these direct movements towards TIII occurred after TI-instructed trials.
evidence: Quantitative result about trial sequence effects.

claim: 91.67% of direct movements towards TIII occurred after TII- or TIII-instructed trials.
source: In the remaining 91.67% of the trials, direct movements towards TIII occurred after TII- or TIII-instructed trials, which required the activation of MU2 to reach the target.
evidence: Quantitative result about trial sequence effects.

claim: During direct movement towards TIII, MU2 was recruited on average at a 48.43 ± 22.46% lower force level than during ramp recruitment.
source: During direct movement towards TIII, MU2 was recruited on average at a 48.43 ± 22.46% lower force level than during ramp recruitment.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of force levels during different recruitment conditions.

claim: The global EMG values at recruitment of MU2 were, on average, slightly lower during direct movements towards TIII (TA: –15.91 ± 9.67%; FL: –18.75 ± 23.27%; GL: –9.99 ± 31.53%; GM: –0.02 ± 27.31%).
source: Also, the global EMG values at recruitment of MU2 were, on average, slightly lower during direct movements towards TIII (TA: –15.91 ± 9.67%; FL: –18.75 ± 23.27%; GL: –9.99 ± 31.53%; GM: –0.02 ± 27.31%).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of EMG values during different recruitment conditions.

claim: Across conditions, all subjects used significantly different force levels during each stage of the three-stage approach (Friedman, p<0.001).
source: Across conditions, all subjects used significantly different force levels during each stage (Friedman, p<0.001, two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test Bonferroni-corrected, always p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical result showing differences in force levels across stages.

claim: 24.31% of all indirect target hits of TIII were achieved while MU2 was de-recruited before MU1 during the initial force ramps.
source: Furthermore, for the four subjects for whom the de-recruitment threshold was determined, 24.31% of all indirect target hits of TIII were achieved while MU2 was de-recruited before MU1 during the initial force ramps.
evidence: Quantitative result about de-recruitment patterns during successful trials.

claim: A subtle decrease in force (–0.18 ± 2.33% MVC) was identified when comparing before and after the experiment.
source: A subtle decrease in force (–0.18 ± 2.33% MVC, neither did the de-recruitment force change critically: –0.16 ± 2.28% MVC) and global TA EMG (–2.35 ± 22.62%) were identified.
evidence: Quantitative result comparing pre- and post-experiment measurements.

claim: The global EMG from the lower leg muscles not used for motor unit decomposition increased slightly (FL: 5.45 ± 28.58%; GL: 14.12 ± 37.53%; GM: 18.41 ± 26.51%).
source: However, the global EMG from the lower leg muscles not used for the MU decomposition increased slightly (FL: 5.45 ± 28.58%; GL: 14.12 ± 37.53%; GM: 18.41 ± 26.51%).
evidence: Quantitative result comparing pre- and post-experiment measurements.

claim: The overall recruitment order did not change critically due to the imposed single motor unit modulation.
source: These changes indicate that the overall recruitment order did not change critically due to the imposed single MU modulation.
evidence: Interpretation of the force and EMG measurements.

claim: The increase in activity in the lower leg muscles not directly involved in ankle dorsiflexion relative to the agonist muscle might be explained by induced fatigue towards the end of the experiment.
source: The increase in activity in the lower leg muscles not directly involved in ankle dorsiflexion relative to the agonist muscle might be explained by induced fatigue towards the end of the experiment (Patikas et al., 2002).
evidence: Interpretation of EMG changes with citation to support the explanation.

claim: The rate of agreement between surface and intramuscular EMG decomposition was >94% in the representative validation case.
source: The rate of agreement over the full interval of activity of the MU in this representative case was >94%, which is similar to previous validation results obtained in stable-force conditions (Barsakcioglu et al., 2021).
evidence: Quantitative validation result with reference to Figure 7 and citation.

claim: There were no errors in the first discharges at recruitment and in the last discharges at de-recruitment in the representative validation case.
source: From Figure 7, it can be noted that there were no errors in the first discharges at recruitment and in the last discharges at de-recruitment; therefore, onset and offset of this MU activity were detected highly accurately.
evidence: Observation from validation data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The rate of agreement during the ramp-up phase was 91.7% in the representative validation case.
source: The ramp-up phase of this MU activity lasted between 12.1 and 15.0 s of the contraction time and in this phase the rate of agreement was 91.7%.
evidence: Quantitative validation result for specific contraction phase.

claim: The rate of agreement during the constant-force phase was 94.3% in the representative validation case.
source: The constant-force phase of the contraction for this MU lasted from 15.0 to 35.0 s, during which the rate of agreement was 94.3%, and the ramp-down phase lasted between 35.0 and 43.2 s with an estimated accuracy (rate of agreement) of 96.1%.
evidence: Quantitative validation result for specific contraction phase.

claim: The rate of agreement during the ramp-down phase was 96.1% in the representative validation case.
source: The constant-force phase of the contraction for this MU lasted from 15.0 to 35.0 s, during which the rate of agreement was 94.3%, and the ramp-down phase lasted between 35.0 and 43.2 s with an estimated accuracy (rate of agreement) of 96.1%.
evidence: Quantitative validation result for specific contraction phase.

claim: Out of 36 contractions during which validation signals were recorded, common motor units were detected in only 16 contractions.
source: Out of the 36 contractions during which validation signals were recorded (three subjects, six slopes, two trials per slope), common MUs were detected in only 16 contractions.
evidence: Quantitative result from validation study.

claim: In all cases in which common motor units were detected, the rate of agreement was >90%.
source: In all cases in which common MUs were detected, the rate of agreement was >90% and the errors in decomposition were equally distributed in all phases of the contractions (on average, 93.2 ± 1.3%, 92.6 ± 1.5%, and 95.5 ± 2.0% for the three phases of the contraction, respectively), without any preferential distribution around the intervals of recruitment and de-recruitment.
evidence: Quantitative validation result across all validation cases.

claim: No error was observed in the first discharge (onset) or the last discharge (offset) in the validation study.
source: Notably, we never observed an error in the first discharge (onset) or the last discharge (offset), meaning that the recruitment and de-recruitment times were detected by the online decomposition with an accuracy of 1 ms (margin used in the time alignment between discharge times detected by the surface and intramuscular decomposition).
evidence: Validation result about accuracy of onset and offset detection.

claim: The online surface EMG decomposition in variable force contractions with recruitment and de-recruitment achieved similar performance as the decomposition in static contractions.
source: From the validation tests, we concluded that the online surface EMG decomposition in variable force contractions with recruitment and de-recruitment achieved similar performance as the decomposition in static contractions.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from validation study results.

claim: Subjects could gain control over four motor units from a single muscle.
source: Our results showed that subjects could gain control over four MUs from a single muscle.
evidence: Summary of main experimental finding in the Discussion.

claim: Subjects did not exploit potential neural structures with selective inputs to individual motor units.
source: Therefore, subjects did not exploit potential neural structures with selective inputs to individual MUs.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Low-threshold motor units active at low force levels may be more prone to the effect of sustained persistent inward currents.
source: These low-threshold MUs active at such force levels may be more prone to the effect of sustained PICs (Heckman et al., 2008b), which might explain the hysteresis between recruitment and de-recruitment threshold observed for most MUs examined in this experiment.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental observations with citation.

claim: An inhibitory input is needed to extinguish the impact of persistent inward currents on motor unit discharge behavior.
source: An inhibitory input is needed to extinguish the impact of PICs on the MU discharge behaviour (Heckmann et al., 2005).
evidence: Statement about physiological mechanism with citation.

claim: Persistent inward currents act diffusely across the entire motor unit pool.
source: PICs act diffuse across the entire MU pool (Johnson and Heckman, 2014).
evidence: Statement about physiological mechanism with citation.

claim: The broad influence of persistent inward currents may be focalized by local inhibition, which allows suppression of the PIC effect on selective motor unit pools and sub-pools.
source: However, it may be possible that the broad influence of PICs is focalised by local inhibition, which allows suppression of the PIC effect on selective MU pools and sub-pools (Heckman et al., 2008a).
evidence: Statement about potential physiological mechanism with citation.

claim: Synaptic inhibition received by motor neurons follows the size principle.
source: Synaptic inhibition received by motor neurons follows the size principle. Hence, smaller motor neurons tend to show a greater hyperpolarisation than larger ones for the same inhibitory input (Henneman et al., 1965; Heckman and Binder, 1988).
evidence: Statement about physiological mechanism with citations.

claim: Smaller motor neurons tend to show a greater hyperpolarization than larger ones for the same inhibitory input.
source: Synaptic inhibition received by motor neurons follows the size principle. Hence, smaller motor neurons tend to show a greater hyperpolarisation than larger ones for the same inhibitory input (Henneman et al., 1965; Heckman and Binder, 1988).
evidence: Statement about physiological consequence with citations.

claim: A mixture of broadly distributed neuromodulatory mechanisms and locally acting inhibition may have produced the variability in motor unit activity observed in this study.
source: However, we consider that it is likely that a mixture of broadly distributed neuromodulatory mechanisms, such as PICs, and locally acting inhibition may have produced the variability in MU activity that was observed in this study.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: Similar findings on the increasing variability in motor unit activation by incorporating neuromodulation and inhibition have been shown in a simulation study.
source: Similar findings on the increasing variability in MU activation by incorporating neuromodulation and inhibition have been shown in a simulation study (Powers et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to simulation study.

claim: A direct proof of altered motor unit recruitment as a consequence of independent input to different motor units needs to be provided during the initial activation phase.
source: Therefore, a direct proof of altered MU recruitment as a consequence of independent input to different MUs needs to be provided during the initial activation phase, that is, an MU with higher recruitment threshold activated before an MU with lower threshold without preceding activations.
evidence: Methodological requirement stated for proving flexible motor unit control.

claim: The study did not get results supporting a general flexible control of motor units.
source: We did not get results supporting a general flexible control of MUs, that is, volitional activation of higher threshold MUs before lower threshold ones at initial recruitment.
evidence: Summary of negative finding from the study.

claim: Subjects learned to establish universal control strategies that allowed for the achievement of the target task for various combinations of motor units.
source: Hence, these findings suggest that subjects learned to establish universal control strategies that allowed for the achievement of the target task for various combinations of MUs.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results.

claim: The sole activation of a higher threshold motor unit was only possible by exploiting the history-dependent activation of motor units.
source: Therefore, the sole activation of a higher threshold MU was only possible by exploiting the history-dependent activation of MUs, that is, exclusive firing of MU2 follows the combined activation of MU1 and MU2.
evidence: Conclusion about the mechanism enabling selective motor unit activation.

claim: A more efficient strategy of directly activating MU2 without a preceding activation of MU1 was not feasible for the subjects.
source: The results suggest that this three-stage approach to achieve a hit in TIII as quickly as possible was feasible for the subjects while a more efficient strategy of directly activating MU2 without a preceding activation of MU1 was not.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results about control strategies.

claim: Subjects can learn to control motor units independently when exposed to biofeedback on the discharge behavior.
source: It has been previously shown that subjects can learn to control MUs independently when exposed to biofeedback on the discharge behaviour (Formento et al., 2021; Basmajian, 1963).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citations.

claim: Variations in force directions potentially have an impact on the recruitment order.
source: Such variations in force directions (ter Haar Romeny et al., 1984; Desnedt and Gidaux, 1981) but also other motor behavioural changes, including alternations in postures (Nardone et al., 1989), and contraction speed (Desmedt and Godaux, 1977a), potentially have an impact on the recruitment order.
evidence: Statement about factors affecting recruitment order with citations.

claim: Independent control of individual motor units would imply that a motor unit can be controlled independently of all other motor units.
source: Indeed, independent control of individual MUs would imply that an MU can be controlled independently of all other MUs.
evidence: Definition of what constitutes independent motor unit control.

claim: A recent study in humans provided evidence for the existence of motor unit pool synergies similar to the functional grouping of muscles involved in a single movement.
source: A recent study in humans provided evidence for the existence of MU pool synergies similar to the functional grouping of muscles involved in a single movement (Tanzarella et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement about prior research with citation.

claim: The central nervous system may send a common input to motor unit pool synergies, which are not per se limited to innervating only a single muscle.
source: The CNS may send a common input to these MU pool synergies, which are not per se limited to innervating only a single muscle (Laine et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about motor control organization with citation.

claim: The tibialis anterior muscle has properties that facilitate a reliable decomposition of motor unit activity using surface recordings.
source: Here, we extracted single MU activity from the TA since this muscle has properties (e.g. muscle fibres arrangement, proximity to the skin, distribution of innervation zones) that facilitate a reliable decomposition of MU activity using surface recordings (Barsakcioglu et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2022; Negro et al., 2016a; Dideriksen et al., 2018; Del Vecchio et al., 2020) and a relatively large number of monosynaptic connections with the motor cortex that could potentially be leveraged for direct independent MU control (Ibáñez et al., 2021; Dideriksen et al., 2018).
evidence: Justification for muscle selection with multiple citations.

claim: The tibialis anterior has a relatively large number of monosynaptic connections with the motor cortex.
source: Here, we extracted single MU activity from the TA since this muscle has properties (e.g. muscle fibres arrangement, proximity to the skin, distribution of innervation zones) that facilitate a reliable decomposition of MU activity using surface recordings (Barsakcioglu et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2021; Bräcklein et al., 2022; Negro et al., 2016a; Dideriksen et al., 2018; Del Vecchio et al., 2020) and a relatively large number of monosynaptic connections with the motor cortex that could potentially be leveraged for direct independent MU control (Ibáñez et al., 2021; Dideriksen et al., 2018).
evidence: Anatomical fact about the tibialis anterior with citations.
